sources.description: In February that year, the Slovenian government officially deleted 25,000 citizens, turning them overnight into illegal immigrants So much of your daily life – your job, your health, your home – hinges on the fact that your name is in a government database. Are you a legal citizen of your country, with everything that entails? You are, until an anonymous bureaucrat hits a key one night and strips it all away, turning you into an illegal immigrant. It happened in Slovenia in 1992. “I took my son to register for secondary school. The clerk rifled through the papers, then stared at me as if refusing to see the boy standing right next to me. Finally, she said: ‘But you don’t have a son. He doesn’t exist.’” I can’t forget the look on the face of the woman who was telling me this story. It was a mixture of deep hurt and bewilderment, with a pause after every sentence, as if she were walking through a minefield. During the research for my book Erased, I compiled countless stories like this: stories I once would have thought impossible. sources.title: 向胜利纪念碑发难，日本安的什么心？ | 新漫评
sources.description: 近日，俄罗斯哈巴罗夫斯克一座纪念战胜日本军国主义的纪念碑正式揭幕。15米高的红军战士雕像，以枪托砸碎刻有日本菊花纹章的界碑。日本首相高市早苗与日本外务省随即提出抗议，声称菊花纹章是日本象征，要求俄方拆除纪念碑。俄外交部发言人扎哈罗娃回应，拆除纪念碑的要求“如同妄想风停、日息”，俄罗斯的历史根植于事实，民族记忆凝固在纪念碑之上。
